opus-5.5.text:
I think it's natural because linear attention is, at its core, a very mathematical object. When you remove the softmax from standard attention, what you're left with is essentially a sequence of matrix products, and the whole point of the field is to exploit the algebraic structure that appears once that nonlinearity is gone. You can reorder the computation thanks to associativity, so instead of forming the full attention matrix you maintain a fixed-size state that gets updated at every step. Once you see it that way, linear attention becomes a kind of linear recurrent neural network, and to describe that recurrence precisely you need formulas.

There's also a lot happening at different levels. There's the recurrent form, which is good for inference. There's the parallel form, which looks like masked attention. And there's the chunkwise form, which sits in between and is what you actually want for efficient training on GPUs. Showing that these three are equivalent, and deriving how to move between them, especially when you add things like decay terms, gating, or the delta rule, requires careful derivation. With something like DeltaNet, for example, the state update involves a Householder-like transition, and parallelizing it over the sequence means using tools like the WY representation from numerical linear algebra. You can't explain that convincingly in words alone.

And finally, a lot of the progress in this area comes from noticing connections: that a model's update rule is online gradient descent on some objective, or that different architectures are special cases of one framework with different structured transition matrices. Those unifying views are naturally expressed in math. So I think the formulas aren't decoration. They're really the language that lets you see why these models work, how they relate to each other, and how to make them hardware efficient. For me, the math is often where the ideas actually come from.

r001.rationale: The response says linear attention reduces to a sequence of matrix products and relies on the algebraic structure of those transformations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the recurrent, parallel, and chunkwise forms are equivalent, including the recurrent and chunkwise forms named in the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's natural because the whole point of linear attention is a mathematical reformulation. Standard softmax attention is simple to write down, but the softmax is exactly what prevents you from reordering the computation. Once you remove it, you can use the associativity of matrix multiplication to change the order in which things are computed, and suddenly you have a recurrence instead of a quadratic attention over the whole sequence. That transformation is algebra. There is no way to explain it honestly without writing the equations.

And the formulas carry real information. When you write the recurrent form, the chunk-wise form, and the parallel form side by side, each one tells you something different about the model. The recurrent form tells you what the state is and how big it is. The parallel form tells you how it relates to attention. The chunk-wise form is what you actually implement in a kernel, because that is what maps well onto tensor cores. If I only described this in words, you would get the intuition but you would not be able to implement it or see where the memory and compute actually go.

There is also a practical reason. Many of the improvements in this area, things like gating, decay, delta rule updates, are small changes in one line of the recurrence. If the paper is written mostly in prose, these differences look trivial or get lost. In the formulas you can see exactly what changed and why it matters for hardware efficiency or expressivity. So for me the math is not decoration, it is the content. The algorithm and the equations are the same object.

r001.rationale: The response explains that linear attention depends on algebraic reformulation and reordering matrix computations, making equations necessary to describe it.

astra-6.text: I think it’s natural because linear attention is fundamentally about changing how a mathematical operation is computed. You need formulas to make clear what you’re changing, why it reduces the computational cost, and what happens to the model’s behavior. With attention, even a change in the order of operations can be central to the method, and an equation can express that much more precisely than a paragraph. The important thing is that the formulas support a clear intuition, so readers can understand both what the method does and why it makes sense.
